power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Non-ventilator-associated hospital-acquired pneumonia (nv-HAP) diagnosis is imprecise; chest x-rays (CXR) lack detail and sputum culture delays targeted prescribing.
However, the evidence base to support diagnostic improvement is sparse.
We assessed the feasibility of a trial of low-dose thoracic CT and rapid molecular testing of sputum.
HAP-FAST was a UK NIHR funded, open-label pilot sequential multiple assignment randomised trial with qualitative and costing substudies in four UK hospitals (ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT05483309).

Using research without prior consent (RWPC) and sitestratified web-based randomisation, clinicians allocated adults with suspected nv-HAP (excluding pregnancy and palliation), before their second antibiotic dose, 1:1 to CT or CXR; participants subsequently treated for nv-HAP with sputum available underwent another 1:1 randomisation to BIOFIRE FILMARRAY Pneumonia plus Panel (FAPP) with standard microbiology or standard microbiology alone .
Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, consent, intervention delivery and data completeness through 90 days.
Adverse events were not systematically collected.
Analyses were intention-to-treat and descriptive.
Between June 2023 and March 2024, 220 adults were randomised at stage-1 (109 CT; 111 CXR), reaching target three months early.
Of 154/220 (70.0%) subsequently managed as nv-HAP, 92/154 (59.7%) could not produce sputum.
62/154 (40.3%; 28.2% of stage-1) were randomised to stage-2: 31 FAPP and 31 no-FAPP.
Allocated imaging was recorded for 75/109 (68.8%) CT and 99/111 (89.2%) CXR participants; 6/31(19.4%) FAPP tests were not completed.
Consent for follow-up was obtained for 142/220 (64.5%).
Protocol-defined clinical cure was assessable in 1/220 participants.
The day-90 resource-use questionnaire was returned by 55/110 participants (50.0%).
Qualitative findings supported RWPC but identified needs for staged communication, lower-burden follow-up and improved diagnostic pathways.
Excess bed days and readmissions drove costs but data capture requires refinement.
A definitive trial is plausible only with enhanced RWPC, diagnostic delivery and follow-up pathways, improved sputum procedures, stewardship-aligned outcomes and routine economic data capture.
Evidence to guide diagnostic strategies for suspected nv-HAP is limited, and the feasibility of evaluating sequential imaging and rapid sputum testing is uncertain.
HAP-FAST showed that recruitment to a sequential diagnostic trial was achievable, but identified important limitations in intervention delivery, follow-up and outcome assessment.
Integrated qualitative and costing findings explained priorities for redesign.
A definitive trial should incorporate staged consent, reliable diagnostic pathways, lowerburden follow-up, feasible clinical and stewardship outcomes, and improved resource-use measurement.

Non-ventilator-associated hospital-acquired pneumonia (nv-HAP) is the most common healthcare-associated infection and causes substantial mortality, prolongs admission and increases costs. 1, 2 Guidelines recommend broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics. 3 Stewardship depends on correctly identifying nv-HAP as the cause of the patient's deterioration and identifying pathogens early enough to guide treatment.

Establishing whether clinicians can recruit, deliver the tests and collect interpretable outcomes is therefore necessary before evaluating effectiveness.

text.text: Patient and public representatives reviewed drafts of the original grant proposal and influenced the final study design.
They contributed during protocol development by reviewing the protocol and study documents and suggesting changes.
They served on trial oversight committees and contributed to interpretation of findings and manuscript review.
A public contributor reviewed the qualitative topic guides before data collection.
In addition, patients and their relatives and friends who had direct lived experience of participation in the trial participated in qualitative interviews.
Patients and public representatives reviewed and commented upon this manuscript and are named authors.
HAP-FAST was an open-label pilot sequential multiple assignment randomised trial (SMART), coordinated by Liverpool Clinical Trials Centre (LCTC), in four acute hospitals in north-west England.

The protocol was published previously. 16 The target of 220 participants over 12 months was based on prospective audits at two centres, assuming 30% eligibility and 40% recruitment. 16 The planned recruitment period allowed assessment across seasons and different hospital contexts.

text.text: Two sequential decisions were evaluated: stage-1 imaging (CXR versus low-dose thoracic CT) and stage-2 microbiological investigation with or without the BIOFIRE FILMARRAY Pneumonia plus Panel (FAPP).
These defined four dynamic treatment regimens: CXR/no-FAPP, CXR/FAPP, CT/no-FAPP and CT/FAPP.
Participants not entering stage-2 remained in follow-up and stage-1 analyses.

Stage-2 randomisation followed the clinician's decision to treat HAP, preserving the sequence of diagnostic decisions rather than assigning all participants to both interventions irrespective of clinical need.
Adults with suspected nv-HAP were eligible if initial trial procedures could be completed before their second antibiotic dose.

In keeping with the definition of nv-HAP used by the UK NICE guidelines, the study included pneumonia developing at least 48 hours after admission or presentation after discharge from an overnight hospital stay within the preceding 10 days.
Exclusions were prior CXR for suspected HAP, ventilator-associated pneumonia, inability to undergo CT, pregnancy, no intention to deliver antibiotics, or previous participation.
Stage-2 eligibility required an intention to treat HAP and sputum availability before the second antibiotic dose.
Baseline sex was self-reported (male/female).

RWPC permitted randomisation and interventions without delaying treatment. 12 Written informed consent for continued participation was sought as soon as practicable; personal or professional consultees were involved when participants lacked capacity.

text.text: An independent statistician generated site-stratified allocation schedules with variable block sizes, held centrally by LCTC and concealed until web-based allocation.
Clinicians could confirm eligibility and randomise at any time.
Stage-1 allocation was 1:1 to CXR or CT; stage-2 allocation was 1:1 to FAPP plus standard microbiology or standard microbiology alone.
Allocations were immediately revealed and notified to clinicians because results informed care.
After stage-1 imaging, managing clinicians interpreted CXRs and radiologists reported CTs urgently.
For stage-2, instruments were placed in clinical areas and operated by clinicians; three sites used the FILMARRAY TORCH and one site used the FILMARRAY 2.0.
FAPP results were interpreted using an antibiotic guideline approved by all sites.
Participants in the no-FAPP arm received empirical antibiotics according to local guidelines.
After consent, CAP-Sym symptom and EQ-5D-5L quality-of-life questionnaires were collected where feasible. 19, 20 Baseline clinical data included medical history and medication use.

text.text: Daily reviews assessed clinical cure, with subsequent follow-up capturing symptoms, quality of life and further resource use.
Participants were reviewed daily until day 10 or discharge, at day 28 in person and day 90 by telephone.
Mechanistic research sampling is reported separately.
We purposively sampled patients, personal consultees and practitioners across sites, roles and participant characteristics.
Patients and consultees were contacted at least two weeks after discharge for semi-structured interviews at home or by telephone.
Practitioners were recruited through site investigators for face-to-face or online focus groups, supplemented by interviews to include under-represented roles or sites.
A non-clinical qualitative researcher conducted all interviews and focus groups after separate informed consent.
A public contributor reviewed topic guides before data collection; guides were iteratively refined during analysis.
Verbatim transcripts were checked against recordings and pseudonymised.
Collaborative reflexive thematic analysis proceeded alongside data collection. 21 The qualitative researcher led coding in NVivo whilst a clinician-trialist separately reviewed all transcripts.

text.text: Patient, consultee and practitioner datasets were initially analysed separately, then compared across groups.
Analytic discussions challenged and refined interpretations rather than establishing coding agreement.
Findings are presented alongside quantitative process measures to explain feasibility constraints and identify design implications.

The primary objective was feasibility, including recruitment, consent, representativeness, retention to day 90, intervention delivery, outcome completeness, acceptability, decisionmaking and economic data capture.

Several potential outcome measures for a future fully powered trial were considered (hereafter referred to as 'candidate outcomes'): clinical cure, antibiotic defined daily doses (DDD), EQ-5D-5L, length of stay and mortality at days 14, 28 and 90.

The prespecified clinical cure outcome, developed from Weiss et al., required at least 35% improvement in symptoms measured by CAP-Sym, clinical stability using modified Halm's criteria, and radiological stability or improvement at days 7-10. 14, 20, 22 Additional imaging findings, FAPP pathogens and UK-AWaRe antibiotic categories were described. 23 Feasibility assessment also considered descriptive estimates and dispersion of candidate outcomes, clinician willingness to randomise, human factors affecting test delivery and factors influencing follow-up.

text.text: Formal progression thresholds were not prespecified; given the novelty and complexity of HAP-FAST, feasibility was assessed holistically rather than by applying retrospective numerical thresholds.
Adverse events were not systematically collected, as prespecified in the protocol.
Analyses followed the prespecified statistical analysis plan (supplementary file) after 90-day follow-up, without interim analyses.
Stage-specific comparisons were by intention-to-treat regardless of deviations and were descriptive, without hypothesis testing.
Missingness was reported.
Real-time eligibility confirmation replaced conventional screening logs, so population denominators for eligibility, approach and recruitment were unavailable.

Representativeness was assessed against site-coded nv-HAP episodes in the routinely collected NHS Secondary Uses Service (SUS) database and the clinically validated Advancing Quality (AQ) sample, recognising possible ICD-10 miscoding. [24] [25] [26] Analyses used SAS 9.4 and R 4.4.1.

text.text: The fourth qualitative theme concerned pathway fit.
CT delivery was constrained by transfer logistics and tolerance of lying flat, rather than rejection of the trial concept or lack of equipoise.
FAPP delivery required successful sputum collection, sample handling, access to equipment, testing ownership and communication of results to clinical teams.
These accounts explain how rapid tests can remain operationally fragile despite short analytical turnaround and identify modifiable steps between allocation and treatment decisions.
Staff valued the prospect of pathogen-directed treatment, and patients and consultees supported appropriate antibiotic use.

However, practitioners described the work involved in obtaining, analysing, transferring and interpreting the results, suggesting that influence on prescribing depended on information being early, trusted and linked to clinical review.

text.text: Protocol-defined clinical cure was assessable in only 1/220 participants; 219/220 (99.5%) lacked assessment, mainly because repeat imaging was unavailable at days 7-10.
A post-hoc definition omitting radiology yielded cure in 15/109 (13.8%) CT and 12/111 (10.8%) CXR participants, and 9/31 (29.0%) FAPP and 7/31 (22.6%) no-FAPP participants.
Substantial non-assessment remained: 73/109 CT and 67/111 CXR participants, and 8/31 FAPP and 15/31 no-FAPP participants, could not be assessed using the relaxed definition.
Reasons for non-assessment including missing symptom or consent-related data are detailed in SAR tables 12-4 and 12-19.
Mean antibiotic DDDs were 4.0 (SD 7.2) with CT, 4.8 (9.1) with CXR, 7.1 (9.4) with FAPP and 5.4 (7.9) without FAPP; missingness was substantial.
DDD data were missing for 21/109 CT, 10/111 CXR, 7/31 FAPP and 8/31 no-FAPP participants (table 3).
UK-AWaRe distributions were broadly similar at stage-1.
Reserve use, exclusively meropenem, occurred in 6/109 (5.5%) CT and 9/111 (8.1%) CXR participants; at stage-2, it occurred in 8/31 (25.8%) FAPP participants and none without FAPP.
EQ-5D visual analogue scale (VAS) estimates were limited by incomplete follow-up.
Mean baseline-to-day-90 changes were 7.7 points with CT and 5.4 with CXR; corresponding changes were 25.9 with FAPP and 15.7 without FAPP.

Between-arm differences in VAS change, estimated using linear regression adjusted for baseline VAS score, were -0.9 points (95% CI -16.6 to 14.8) for CT versus CXR and 17.7 (-6.0 to 41.4) for FAPP versus no-FAPP.
Median post-HAP length of stay was 19 days (IQR 8-52) with CT and 13 (6-42) with CXR; corresponding stage-2 values were 9 (7-16) and 17 (9-not estimable).
Long stays resulted in censoring.
By day 90, 29/220 stage-1 participants had died, with 80 censored (predominantly due to withdrawal of consent).
Kaplan-Meier survival was 80.7% (95% CI 68.9-88.4) with CT and 79.8% (69.1-87.1) with CXR.
No deaths were observed in the FAPP arm, with 5/31 censored, versus 8/31 deaths and 7/31 censored without FAPP.
In the no-FAPP arm, four deaths were recorded by day 14 and five by day 28.
Reported causes and timing of deaths are provided in SAR table 7-2.

text.text: Available-case mean inpatient costs per participant were £9,187 with CT and £9,806 with CXR.
In the smaller stage-2 subset, mean inpatient costs were higher without FAPP (£9,127 versus £7,261 with FAPP), largely reflecting excess bed days.
Readmissions and community services accounted for 80.0% and 11.4% of aggregate recorded postdischarge costs, respectively.
HAP-FAST demonstrated successful recruitment to a sequential diagnostic trial in suspected nv-HAP but identified why a definitive trial should not simply enlarge this protocol.

When managing suspected nv-HAP imaging and microbiology address linked decisions: whether nv-HAP explains a patient's deterioration and which antibiotic should be chosen to target the responsible pathogen.

The SMART design followed this sequence, while embedded qualitative and costing evidence explained implementation constraints that recruitment totals alone could obscure. 17, 18 The central finding is therefore conditional feasibility, not evidence of clinical or economic effectiveness.

text.text: The recruitment target was reached early.

Radiological tests performed at stage-1 successfully excluded a diagnosis of nv-HAP in 30% of participants thus after further excluding those who could not produce sputum, 28% of participants randomized at stage-1 entered stage-2.
This proportion is essential for sample-size planning but limits generalisability of microbiological comparisons to the 40% of sputum-producing patients with radiologically confirmed nv-HAP.
The qualitative finding of conditional acceptance helps distinguish willingness to enter an urgent diagnostic pathway from willingness to undertake repeated research procedures.
Blood sampling and in-person follow-up discouraged continued participation; future designs should minimise non-essential sampling and use remote follow-up where feasible.
RWPC and clinician-led randomisation accommodated urgent treatment, ward dispersion and cognitive impairment without requiring specialist research staff on every ward continuously.

Interviews supported RWPC but identified the need for staged explanations, later recap and consultee support. 28 Acceptability should therefore be treated as an ongoing process rather than inferred from recruitment alone.
text.formatted: Interviews supported RWPC but identified the need for staged explanations, later recap and consultee support. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">28</ref> Acceptability should therefore be treated as an ongoing process rather than inferred from recruitment alone.

text.text: The limited qualitative representation of people who did not consent further cautions against assuming universal acceptance.
A definitive trial should distinguish agreement to routine-data follow-up from agreement to additional questionnaires, visits or samples wherever its consent arrangements permit.
Imaging findings illustrate the importance of separating delivery from documentation.
Recorded CT receipt was incomplete, with missing forms contributing substantially to apparent non-delivery.
Although recorded scans and reports were generally rapid, practitioners described scanner prioritisation, transfer logistics and tolerance as constraints.

Future site-readiness assessments need explicit radiology agreements covering transfer, reporting and incidental findings, together with reliable delivery recording and allowance for crossover or non-receipt in design and analysis.
The longer formal CXR reporting interval should not be equated with delayed interpretation, because managing clinicians interpreted CXR directly.
FAPP implementation was more fragile.
Locating instruments near patients and training clinicians did not remove dependencies on sputum production, sample transfer, test ownership, result communication and antibiotic decision making.
Qualitative accounts related recruitment decisions, sample losses and test non-completion to these practical steps.
Future trials should implement systems for remote results access and antibiotic decision support, linking timely results to explicit stewardship review.
Improved analytical speed alone does not ensure that diagnostic information reaches decision-makers or changes treatment.
Outcome measurement was a major feasibility result.
The prespecified clinical-cure composite was effectively unusable because in clinical practice repeat imaging is rarely performed within days 7-10.
Removing radiology post-hoc increased the proportion assessable but did not completely resolve missingness.

Symptom data collected during days 0-10 may help characterise recovery and inform future assessment timepoints and thresholds, but this would require further evaluation rather than treating the exploratory definition as a validated endpoint.

CAP-derived symptom and physiological criteria may not transfer readily to this population. 14, 15, 20, 22 Cognitive impairment complicates self-report, while participants with an alternative diagnosis to pneumonia still require appropriate stage-1 outcomes.

text.text: A future endpoint should therefore be diagnosis-agnostic, objective, routinely collected and suitable for an open-label trial; NEWS2 warrants evaluation.
Antibiotic stewardship outcomes may better match the mechanism of diagnostic intervention, but DDD alone does not distinguish appropriate escalation from avoidable exposure.
The higher DDDs and 'Reserve' class antibiotic use seen with FAPP cannot establish benefit or harm: rapid microbiology results may prompt justified escalation as well as de-escalation.

Related studies show these context-dependent prescribing effects and uncertainty around clinical endpoints. 9, 29 A stewardship-focused outcome paired with safety or clinical response deserves evaluation. 30 Outcome selection should precede definitive sample-size calculation, rather than relying on unstable effect estimates from this pilot.

text.text: Length of stay and quality-of-life measures provided planning information, but missingness, censoring and small stage-2 groups limit interpretation.

Similar demographics in our comparator cohorts are reassuring, not proof of representativeness since HAP-FAST recruited when nv-HAP was suspected, whereas SUS and AQ capture coded and confirmed nv-HAP respectively.
Apparent differences in outcomes across these sources may therefore reflect case definition as well as recruitment.
Without screening denominators, recruitment may still depend on recognition timing, CT tolerance, clinician availability and sputum production.
Mortality differences observed in these small, incompletely followed groups do not support effectiveness conclusions but are valuable for future trial planning.

The 50% post-discharge costing questionnaire return and available-case costing create potential selection biases, beyond item-level missingness so data inform future measurement rather than prove cost-effectiveness.
Assistance with completion or routine-data extraction should be tested for acceptability and completeness, not assumed to solve missingness automatically.

The CAP-NEXT community-acquired pneumonia study also encountered incomplete delivery of low-dose CT and molecular testing, suggesting that diagnostic information must be integrated with workflow and prescribing decisions. 31 That study stopped early during

text.text: COVID-19 and did not collect reasons for non-adherence.
HAP-FAST's qualitative component addresses this explanatory gap for a different pneumonia population, linking observed failures to practical delivery conditions and participant experience.
HAP-FAST adds nv-HAP-specific evidence by connecting quantitative delivery and retention measures with patient, consultee and practitioner accounts.
Strengths include this integration, pragmatic sequential randomisation and evaluation of RWPC in a pneumonia trial outside critical care.
Limitations include incomplete interventions and outcomes, available-case costing, absent screening logs and limited qualitative representation from non-consenters.

Progression is therefore conditional on redesign: enhanced RWPC, protected diagnostic pathways, enhanced sputum procedures, lower-burden follow-up, diagnosis-agnostic and stewardship-aligned outcomes, and robust economic data capture.
A definitive trial should consider an internal pilot with prespecified stop-go criteria for recruitment, intervention delivery, outcome completeness and costing.
Qualitative evaluation should remain integrated to explain whether refinements work, for whom and under which delivery conditions, informing implementation in clinical practice.

Qualitative data comprised 23 patient-linked interviews with 24 participants (20 patients and four personal consultees), including one joint patient-consultee interview.
Twenty practitioners participated in four site-based focus groups and four individual interviews.
Four themes contextualised trial delivery; illustrative quotations are in table 2.
The first theme was conditional acceptance of recruitment.

Patients and consultees supported participation perceived as low-burden, clinically sensible and optional, but decisions during acute illness were often trust-based, altruistic or instinctive rather than demonstrating detailed understanding.

The second concerned RWPC: this was broadly considered necessary, but acceptability depended on staged communication, later recap, clearer consultee support and separation of research from routine care.
These findings contextualise consent rates without equating initial recruitment with informed willingness to continue.
Practitioner accounts distinguished objections to later study demands from objections to RWPC itself.
Patients and relatives described the need to revisit information because explanations given during acute illness might not be retained.
Thus, a successful first approach did not remove the need for subsequent support and clarification.

The third qualitative theme explained cumulative retention barriers.
Participants and practitioners described repeated questionnaires and blood tests, travel, parking and uncertainty about appointment purpose as disincentives and reasons for withdrawal.
Accounts included participants prioritising unencumbered recovery over multiple assessments, and practical difficulties attending hospital after discharge.
